label: Verve
rationale: The record that made bossa nova a permanent part of the jazz language, and by most counts the best-selling and most-consensus jazz album of the 1960s. Getz/Gilberto won the 1965 Grammy for Album of the Year — the first non-American album ever to do so — plus Best Jazz Instrumental Album and Best Engineered Recording, and it sits on Rolling Stone's and Vibe's all-time best-albums lists. Session gravity is unusual and specific: Stan Getz (the canon's cool-jazz tenor voice, already load-bearing here), João Gilberto (bossa nova's inventor, guitar+vocal), Antônio Carlos Jobim (the music's great composer, at the piano), and Astrud Gilberto's career-launching vocals on 'The Girl from Ipanema'. Lineage is everywhere — the whole 1960s–70s jazz/latin conversation runs through it, and it still plays: 'Corcovado' and 'Desafinado' remain touchstones. This is a defining statement of a scene and a consensus core record, not a novelty.

personnel_record.notes: Recorded March 18–19, 1963 at A & R Recording, New York City (Phil Ramone's studio), released March 1964 on Verve. Two consecutive days, one studio, one ensemble — treated as a single session. Bassist conflict: reissues credit Tommy Williams, but recording-session photos (Castro 1990) and AllMusic confirm Sebastião Neto; the conflict is preserved here. Astrud Gilberto sings on two tracks only. Original LP has 8 tracks; later reissues add 45-rpm single versions as bonus tracks (excluded here). Style filed as cool-jazz (Getz's idiom) though the record is the canonical bossa-nova statement — there is no bossa-nova style code in the taxonomy.

ballot.case_for: Getz/Gilberto is the defining statement of the jazz-bossa nova synthesis and a consensus landmark: 1965 Grammy Album of the Year, Best Jazz Instrumental Album, and appearances on Rolling Stone and Vibe all-time lists. It permanently injected João Gilberto's guitar-vocal pulse, Jobim's songbook, and Astrud Gilberto's debut on 'The Girl from Ipanema' into the jazz language, with Stan Getz's cool-toned tenor as the bridge from the post-bebop tradition. Session gravity is unrepeatable — Getz, João Gilberto, Jobim, and Astrud on the same date — and the record's lineage runs through decades of jazz-Latin and lyrical modal playing. Its discovery value remains absolute: 'Corcovado,' 'Desafinado,' and 'The Girl from Ipanema' still teach a curious listener why jazz matters.
ballot.case_against: The strongest counter is genre-purity: a strict constructionist could argue this is fundamentally a Brazilian popular music record featuring a jazz soloist, not a direct extension of the bebop/hard-bop/modal trunk the canon centers on. Its enormous pop success and ubiquity also risk reading as easy-listening crossover rather than the exploratory mid-1960s jazz tradition. The dossier's consensus evidence leans more on Wikipedia, Grammy wins, and broad all-time lists than on explicit Penguin/DownBeat jazz-canon citations, though the cross-platform acclaim partly offsets that. Neither reference found these objections sufficient to move it out of core.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John accept Getz/Gilberto as a consensus-core must-have, with no scope boundary requiring a separate ruling.
